title: At the front door
intro: You reach the door. You can hear everyone already inside, talking before they’ve noticed you’re home.
label: Go in the front door
choice1_text: Walk in and join in like everything’s normal
choice1_pro: You get to just be normal for a minute — no explaining, no big moment, everything carries on like always. That ease is worth something.
choice1_con: Whatever was actually on your mind is still there, quietly, underneath the normal conversation. It hasn’t gone anywhere — it’s just not being said yet.
choice1_tip: If this happens for real: it’s fine to wait for a better moment — just try to actually find that moment later, rather than letting ’later’ quietly become ’never’.
choice2_text: Say what’s actually on your mind
choice2_pro: You just did something genuinely brave — saying a true thing out loud instead of carrying it alone. That’s worth being proud of, whatever happens next.
choice2_con: Saying it can feel exposed for a second — all eyes on you, even if just briefly. That feeling is normal and it passes fast.
choice2_tip: If this happens for real: a simple opener helps — ’can I tell you something?’ — gives the moment space before you say the actual thing.
choice3_text: Go straight to your room instead
choice3_pro: You gave yourself exactly what you needed — space, without having to explain or perform anything first. That’s a real, valid choice.
choice3_con: No one downstairs knows you needed that space, so it might just look like something’s wrong — which could bring more questions later, not fewer.
choice3_tip: If this happens for real: even a single line on the way past — ’just need a minute, I’m okay’ — closes that gap without costing you the space.

title: Around the side
intro: You see it before anyone else has — something’s broken, and it was you. No one else knows yet.
label: Around the side, past the gate
choice1_text: Tell someone straight away, before it’s found
choice1_pro: This is the strongest option there is — you’re the one who said it, not the one who got caught. People remember that difference, and so will you.
choice1_con: There’s a short, real moment right before you say it where your stomach drops a bit. That feeling is just nerves — it’s not a sign you’re doing the wrong thing.
choice1_tip: If this happens for real: starting with ’I need to tell you something’ before the explanation makes it land as honesty, not confession.
choice2_text: Fix it quietly and say nothing
choice2_pro: There’s something genuinely good in quietly making things right without needing anyone to see you do it. That’s real character.
choice2_con: If it IS noticed later, it can look like it was hidden on purpose — even though fixing it wasn’t really hiding. That gap is worth knowing about.
choice2_tip: If this happens for real: fixing it AND mentioning it briefly afterward — ’by the way, I sorted that’ — gets you both things at once.
choice3_text: Wait and see if anyone notices
choice3_pro: Right now, this costs you nothing — no hard conversation, no discomfort today.
choice3_con: The longer it waits, the bigger the moment usually gets when it’s finally found — and things like this are usually found.
choice3_tip: If this happens for real: try setting yourself a short deadline — ’if I haven’t said something by tonight, I will’ — so waiting doesn’t quietly turn into never.

title: Staying in the garden
intro: A couple of kids from school pass the gate. They start having a go — laughing, a comment aimed right at you.
label: Stay right here in the garden
choice1_text: Laugh along like it doesn’t bother you
choice1_pro: It can genuinely take the wind out of it — people often lose interest fast when it doesn’t land the way they wanted.
choice1_con: It still landed on the inside, even while the outside looked fine. Laughing along doesn’t make the sting disappear — it just moves it somewhere harder to see.
choice1_tip: If this happens for real: it’s okay to look fine in the moment AND still tell someone about it afterward — those two things aren’t a contradiction.
choice2_text: Say something back to match them
choice2_pro: There’s something that feels powerful about not just taking it — standing your ground has real value.
choice2_con: This is usually exactly the reaction they were hoping for, and it can turn one comment into a longer back-and-forth that’s harder to walk away from.
choice2_tip: If this happens for real: a short, flat line — ’okay’ — said calmly, does the ’I’m not rattled’ job without giving them more to work with.
choice3_text: Stay calm, say nothing, and walk further into the garden
choice3_pro: This is genuinely the strongest response there is — you gave them nothing to feed off, and you chose where you went. That’s real control, not avoidance.
choice3_con: It can feel hard in the moment to just let a comment sit there unanswered. That discomfort is real — it doesn’t mean you handled it wrong.
choice3_tip: If this happens for real: telling someone about it later still matters, even if you handled the moment itself calmly.

title: One last thing
intro: On your way to bed, you pass the door. Something from earlier is still sitting with you — unsaid.
label: Go back to the door
choice1_text: Go say it now, even though it’s late
choice1_pro: Saying it before you sleep means you’re not carrying it into tomorrow too. That’s worth the extra ten minutes.
choice1_con: It might feel a bit awkward bringing something up right at bedtime — timing isn’t perfect, but perfect timing rarely shows up on its own.
choice1_tip: If this happens for real: even a short version works — ’one more thing before I go up’ — you don’t need the whole conversation, just the start of one.
choice2_pro: Sleep genuinely helps you think more clearly — sometimes morning-you handles it better than tonight-you would.
choice2_con: It’s easy for ’I’ll say it tomorrow’ to quietly turn into not saying it at all, once the moment’s passed.
choice2_tip: If this happens for real: try actually deciding WHEN tomorrow — not just ’sometime’ — so it has a real slot, not just good intentions.
choice3_text: Write it down instead, for now
choice3_pro: This gets it out of your head without needing anyone else awake for it — sometimes that’s exactly the release you need.
choice3_con: Writing it down doesn’t tell the other person anything — it helps you, but the actual gap between you two stays exactly where it was.
choice3_tip: If this happens for real: keep the note somewhere you’ll actually see it tomorrow — otherwise it’s easy to forget it was even there.

title: Lying there
intro: You get into bed. The room’s quiet. Today replays a little in your head.
label: Get into bed
choice1_text: Think about what you’d do the same again
choice1_pro: Noticing what actually worked is just as valuable as noticing what didn’t — it’s how you find out what your strengths already are.
choice1_con: It’s easy to skip past this one because it feels less urgent than the hard parts — worth pausing on anyway.
choice1_tip: Try saying it out loud once, even quietly — ’I think I handled that alright’ — it’s a good habit to practise, not just a hard-day habit.
choice2_text: Think about what you might try differently
choice2_pro: This is where real growth actually happens — not in getting it right first time, in noticing what you’d adjust.
choice2_con: It can start to feel like criticising yourself if you’re not careful — there’s a difference between ’I’d try this instead’ and ’I did it wrong.’
choice2_tip: If this happens for real: you don’t have to act on it tonight. Just noticing it is enough — write it down if it helps it feel finished.
choice3_text: Just let it go and think about something else
choice3_pro: This is a completely valid choice — not every day needs unpacking before you’re allowed to rest.
choice3_con: If this is the choice most nights, even on the harder days, it might be worth noticing whether it’s rest or it’s avoiding.
choice3_tip: If this happens for real: resting is fine. If it’s every single time though, that’s worth mentioning to someone — not because it’s wrong, just worth checking in on.

title: Still awake
intro: You look out at the moon for a minute. Your mind’s still going, even though your body’s tired.
label: Look out at the window
choice1_text: Try to think about something calm on purpose
choice1_pro: Choosing what to think about, on purpose, is a real skill — and it works better than just hoping your brain quiets down by itself.
choice1_con: It doesn’t always work first try — your mind might wander back. That’s normal, not a sign it’s not working.
choice1_tip: If this happens for real: picture somewhere calm in real detail — what you’d see, hear, feel there — detail is what makes it work.
choice2_text: Get up and write the thought down
choice2_pro: Once it’s on paper, your brain doesn’t have to keep holding onto it to make sure it’s not forgotten — that alone can help it quiet down.
choice2_con: Getting up breaks the winding-down feeling for a minute — you’ll need to settle again after.
choice2_tip: If this happens for real: keep paper by the bed so you don’t have to go far — the shorter the interruption, the easier it is to settle back.
choice3_text: Just lie there and let the thoughts keep going
choice3_pro: Sometimes thoughts do actually run their course and quiet down on their own, given enough time.
choice3_con: If this happens most nights and takes a long time to settle, that’s useful information — not something to just push through indefinitely.
choice3_tip: If this happens for real: if it’s most nights, it’s worth mentioning to someone — there are simple things that help, and you don’t have to figure it out alone.

title: The dinner table
intro: Dinner’s on the table. Someone asks ‘how was your day?’ — and just for a second, everyone’s actually listening.
label: Sit down at the table
choice1_pro: Sometimes short is exactly right — not every day needs unpacking at the table, in front of everyone.
choice1_con: If today wasn’t actually fine, this is the moment quietly passing by — it doesn’t come back around the same way later.
choice1_tip: If this happens for real: a short answer now doesn’t rule out a longer one later, one-to-one — ‘can I tell you properly after?’ keeps the door open.
choice2_text: Actually say what today was really like
choice2_pro: This is the whole table hearing it at once — you only have to say it once, not explain it three separate times later.
choice2_con: Saying something real in front of everyone, not just one person, can feel like more eyes on you than you’d planned for.
choice2_tip: If this happens for real: it’s fine to say the short version first, then add ‘actually, can I say more’ — you don’t have to commit to the whole thing in one breath.
choice3_text: Ask someone else about their day instead
choice3_pro: Turning the question around is a genuinely kind thing to do — people notice being asked, and it costs you nothing to offer.
choice3_con: It also means your own day stays exactly where it was — unsaid, whether that was the plan or not.
choice3_tip: If this happens for real: this works well as a stall, not a permanent swap — circle back to your own day once theirs has had its turn.

title: Washing up
intro: Dinner’s finished. The pans are still out. Nobody’s said anything about who’s doing them.
label: Notice the washing up
choice1_text: Offer to do them without being asked
choice1_pro: This is noticed more than almost anything else you could do right now — offering before being asked lands differently than being told to.
choice1_con: It can feel like extra effort right when you’d rather be done for the day — that trade-off is real, not imagined.
choice1_tip: If this happens for real: even doing half and asking for help with the rest still counts as offering — it doesn’t have to be all or nothing.
choice2_text: Wait to see if someone asks you
choice2_pro: There’s nothing wrong with resting after a meal — you’re not obligated to volunteer for every job that shows up.
choice2_con: If everyone’s doing the same ‘waiting to be asked,’ the pans just sit there — someone eventually does them feeling a bit put upon.
choice2_tip: If this happens for real: even a quick ‘shout if you want a hand’ on your way past covers you either way.
choice3_text: Slip off before the question even comes up
choice3_pro: Sometimes you’re genuinely done and need to go — that’s allowed, not everything is a test.
choice3_con: If this is the regular pattern though, it’s usually noticed — quietly, even if nobody says it out loud.
choice3_tip: If this happens for real: if you do need to go, saying so — ‘I’ve got to run, back in a bit’ — reads completely differently to just vanishing.
